facts.title: Named From Wood Ash
facts.text: The English name potassium comes from "potash" — the residue left when you soak wood ash in a pot and boil away the water. Sir Humphry Davy coined the name in 1807 after isolating the metal. The chemical symbol K, however, comes from the Latin "kalium," which itself traces back to the Arabic "al-qali," meaning the calcined ashes of plants.

facts.title: Born From Electricity
facts.text: Potassium was the first metal ever isolated by electrolysis. In October 1807 Humphry Davy passed an electric current from a powerful battery through molten potash and watched tiny shiny globules of a brand-new metal burst into lilac flame. It was one of the very first elements discovered using electrical power rather than chemical reactions alone.

facts.title: A Metal You Can Cut
facts.text: Potassium is astonishingly soft — you can slice it with a butter knife, and a freshly cut surface gleams silvery-white before tarnishing in seconds. It is also lighter than water, with a density of about 0.86 grams per cubic centimetre, so a lump of it actually floats. It is one of only a handful of metals less dense than water.

facts.title: It Sets Water On Fire
facts.text: Drop potassium into water and it reacts violently, fizzing across the surface and igniting the hydrogen gas it releases with a distinctive lilac-purple flame. The reaction is far more vigorous than sodium's and can detonate. This is why potassium metal is stored submerged in mineral oil or kerosene, sealed away from air and moisture.

facts.title: The Purple Flame Test
facts.text: When heated, potassium ions glow a characteristic pale violet or lilac colour, a signature chemists use to identify the element in flame tests. The colour comes from electrons dropping back to lower energy levels and emitting light at specific wavelengths around 766 nanometres. Because sodium's intense yellow can mask it, analysts often view potassium's flame through blue cobalt glass.

facts.title: Essential To Every Heartbeat
facts.text: Potassium is the most abundant positive ion inside your cells, and the flow of potassium across cell membranes generates the electrical signals that fire nerves and contract muscles — including your heart. An adult body holds roughly 120 to 140 grams of it. Both too little and too much in the blood can cause dangerous, even fatal, irregular heartbeats.

facts.title: You Are Slightly Radioactive
facts.text: About 0.012 percent of all natural potassium is the radioactive isotope potassium-40, which decays with a half-life of around 1.25 billion years. Because potassium is in every cell, your own body emits roughly 4,000 to 5,000 radioactive decays per second from it. Geologists use potassium-40's decay into argon-40 to date rocks millions to billions of years old.

facts.title: Feeding The World
facts.text: Potassium is one of the three primary plant nutrients — the "K" in N-P-K fertilizer labels — and roughly 95 percent of mined potash goes into agriculture. Plants need it to regulate water, build proteins, and resist disease. Canada, Russia, and Belarus dominate global potash mining, much of it dug from ancient buried seabeds laid down hundreds of millions of years ago.

facts.title: The Element That Built Banana Myths
facts.text: Bananas are famous for potassium, packing about 358 milligrams per 100 grams, but they are far from the richest source — dried apricots, beans, spinach, and potatoes all contain more. The persistent idea that a banana makes you measurably radioactive is technically true but trivially so. The dose is so tiny it has become a tongue-in-cheek unit called the "banana equivalent dose."

facts.title: Gunpowder's Secret Ingredient
facts.text: Potassium nitrate, also known as saltpetre, makes up about 75 percent of traditional black gunpowder and was prized for centuries as the oxidizer that lets the mixture burn explosively without outside air. The same compound is used today to cure meats, in some fertilizers, and in heat-treating glass. Other potassium salts give fireworks and matches their colour and their spark.
